Context: Human intestinal absorption (HIA) measures the fraction of an orally administered drug absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the portal circulation. This is the first barrier to oral bioavailability — a drug must cross the intestinal epithelium before it encounters hepatic first-pass metabolism. Absorption occurs primarily via passive transcellular diffusion through the lipid bilayer of enterocytes, though carrier-mediated uptake (e.g., PEPT1 for peptide-like drugs, OATP for anionic compounds) and paracellular transport (for very small, hydrophilic molecules) also contribute.

Molecular features favoring high intestinal absorption: moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-4) enables passive diffusion across the enterocyte membrane. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 120 Å²) is one of the strongest predictors — the desolvation cost of burying polar groups in the lipid bilayer is the primary barrier to transcellular transport. Limited hydrogen bond donors (HBD ≤ 3-4) are more important than acceptors because donors form stronger interactions with water that must be broken during membrane partitioning. Features associated with poor absorption: high TPSA (>140 Å²) is the strongest negative predictor. Zwitterionic or multiply charged species at intestinal pH have poor membrane permeability. Very polar, highly hydrophilic molecules (logP < -1) cannot partition into the lipid bilayer. Large, rigid molecules with MW > 600 Da have difficulty crossing the membrane. Compounds subject to active efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp/ABCB1) or BCRP (ABCG2) at the apical enterocyte membrane experience reduced net absorption — Pgp substrates are pumped back into the lumen after partial absorption. This is primarily determined by the molecule's desolvation cost — how much energy is required to strip away the hydration shell of polar groups before entering the hydrophobic membrane interior.

Intramolecular hydrogen bonds can "mask" polar groups and improve permeability beyond what TPSA alone would predict — this is exploited in cyclic peptide drug design.
